newsitem.title: USA: U.S. Senate approves George Tenet as CIA chief.
newsitem.headline: U.S. Senate approves George Tenet as CIA chief.

text.p: The Senate voted late on Thursday to approve President Bill Clinton's nomination of George Tenet as the nation's top spymaster.
The voice vote came after the Senate Intelligence Committee earlier on Thursday unanimously approved the nomination of Tenet, currently deputy director of the Central Intelligence Agency.
Sen. John Warner, a Virginia Republican who knew Tenet when Tenet was a senior staff member on the Senate Intelligence Committee, praised his professional abilities, character and judgment.
"I have confidence in him and I am confident that he will represent our country very well in this important post," Warner said in a statement before the vote.

Clinton tapped Tenet, 44, to become director of central intelligence after Anthony Lake, the president's former national security adviser, withdrew his nomination in frustration over the confirmation process.

Tenet's nomination seemed likely to sail through the Senate intelligence panel, which had earlier confirmed him as deputy CIA director, until the Justice Department began investigating his failure to disclose his part-interest in stocks and real estate inherited from his father.

The Justice Department on Wednesday removed that hurdle when it concluded a preliminary investigation into the matter and said it saw no need to appoint an independent counsel, paving the way for the Senate vote.
Tenet issued a statement moments after the vote, saying he was deeply honoured and vowing to "deliver intelligence that is clear, objective and does not pull punches."
Tenet, who rose smoothly through staff ranks in Congress and the White House to head the U.S. intelligence community, also reiterated a pledge he made to lawmakers during his confirmation hearings.
"You can expect forthright and candid views about our missions, programmes and priorities. I will not hold back," he said.

Tenet was staff director on the Senate Intelligence Committee from 1988 to 1993 under then Chairman David Boren, an Oklahoma Democrat. He was a senior intelligence adviser on the staff of the White House National Security Council from 1993 to 1995.
He became deputy director of central intelligence in July 1995 under then Director John Deutch, who left in December after 20 months in the job, opening the slot for Lake.
In his new job, Tenet will run the CIA and oversee 12 other U.S. spy agencies. In all, the U.S. intelligence operation employs tens of thousands of people and spends about $30 billion a year.
He would be Clinton's third chief spymaster after Deutch and James Woolsey, who quit in December 1994 after becoming entangled in the case of convicted CIA turncoat Aldrich Ames.
In his statement, Tenet pledged to serve the American people with "fidelity, integrity and excellence."
Sen. Richard Shelby, the Alabama Republican who chairs the intelligence committee, said he had hoped to confirm Tenet earlier but needed to await the results of the Justice Department probe.
Shelby said he spoke with Tenet before the vote was taken. "He feels good about this. He's glad it's over with. We are too," Shelby said.

The investigation focused on telephone stock and condominium apartments in Greece that Tenet inherited from his father, who died in 1983. Tenet did not list those items on his initial financial disclosure forms when he joined the Clinton administration.
Tenet said he did not learn about the stock and the Athens property until 1994, when his brother discovered their existence after looking through a family safe deposit box.

Justice Department investigators doubted from the start there would be sufficient evidence to warrant an independent counsel but felt compelled by law to conduct a thorough investigation to make sure, department officials said.
Attorney General Janet Reno approved the decision not to seek an independent counsel, they said.
